title: carboplatin AUC 6 / paclitaxel → dose-dense AC

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin creates links in DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic instructions. Its dose depends on kidney function as well as the intended regimen.
agents.watch: Keep blood-test appointments. Fever, unusual bleeding, repeated vomiting or infusion symptoms need prompt advice.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Allergic reaction, sometimes after previous exposure

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Hair loss, muscle or joint pain
Mouth, bowel, skin and nail effects

agents.name: Doxorubicin
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk.
agents.watch: Report pain or burning at the infusion site immediately. New breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt review. Red urine for a short time can be a drug-colour effect; pain, clots or persistent bleeding still need advice.
risks: Low counts, infection and mouth ulcers
Severe tissue injury if the infusion leaks

agents.name: Cyclophosphamide
agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
agents.watch: Use the prescribed anti-sickness and hydration plan. Report fever, painful urination or blood in the urine.

purpose: Treat the cancer before surgery as part of a plan intended to reduce the risk of it returning.
schedule_summary: Four 21-day cycles: paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15; carboplatin AUC 6 on Day 1. Four further cycles (cycles 5–8): doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 14 days. G-CSF support is required for every dose-dense AC cycle; the team prescribes its product and timing separately. Surgery and pathology review follow chemotherapy. Further systemic treatment, radiotherapy and follow-up depend on the findings and the MDT plan; no routine postoperative immunotherapy is specified by this regimen.

phases_note: The phases run in order. The columns show sequence, not equal time intervals. No dates or other information need to be entered.
timeline_note: Treatment markers show the planned days. Symptom bands are broad possibilities, not measured risk curves; serious symptoms can occur at any time.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
teachback: Which phase are you in, which medicines are active, and what checks are due before the next phase?
consent_support: Discuss treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, common and serious risks, fertility, pregnancy precautions and the full sequence. The treating team completes the individual consent discussion; this guide does not determine personal benefit.
urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

support.title: Separate anti-sickness plans
support.text: The platinum/taxane phase and AC need separate prescriptions. Carboplatin Day 1 uses a high-risk plan; paclitaxel-only Days 8 and 15 use a separate low-risk plan. AC uses its own high-risk plan.

support.title: Growth-factor support
support.text: G-CSF is prescribed for every dose-dense AC cycle. Ask for the exact injection days and instructions.

support.title: Checks before the next dose
support.text: FBC, renal and liver tests weekly throughout chemotherapy, including review before each AC dose. Report new symptoms before the next dose.

support.title: After chemotherapy
support.text: Surgery and pathology review follow chemotherapy. Further systemic treatment, radiotherapy and follow-up depend on the findings and the MDT plan; no routine postoperative immunotherapy is specified by this regimen.

questions.q: When should I call the oncology team?
questions.a: Call immediately for fever, shivers, sudden illness, new breathing difficulty or concerning symptoms. Do not wait for a scheduled blood test or appointment.

questions.q: Why is my chemotherapy changing halfway through?
questions.a: The planned course uses a platinum/taxane phase followed by AC, which works in a different way. The change is part of the pathway and does not by itself mean the first medicines failed.

questions.q: Will I need to enter dates here?
questions.a: No. The maps explain the sequence. Your clinical team provides actual appointment dates.

questions.q: When are ECGs, echoes and blood tests done?
questions.a: Baseline ECG under cardio-oncology guidance (not explicitly listed in NCCP 00348), and cardiac history/risk assessment. NCCP lists baseline echo/MUGA for age over 65 or when clinically indicated. Recheck the cardiac assessment before starting doxorubicin; echo/MUGA during treatment is driven by symptoms, risk or the agreed cardio-oncology plan. There is no automatic three-monthly echo schedule for every person on this pathway. FBC, renal and liver tests weekly throughout chemotherapy, including review before each AC dose.

Chemotherapy comes before surgery. The surgeon discusses lumpectomy or mastectomy as alternatives according to your situation. Radiotherapy, if indicated, follows surgery and recovery; timing is agreed by both teams. It is not automatically given at the same time as these chemotherapy phases.

chapters.title: Why might my team recommend this treatment?
chapters.intro: This is a chemotherapy pathway for triple-negative breast cancer before surgery. Different chemotherapy medicines attack cancer cells in different ways. The team considers cancer extent, previous treatment, kidney and heart health, fitness and whether a chemotherapy-only approach fits the individual plan. This card does not decide whether immunotherapy should be added.

items.title: Your treatment aim
items.text: Treat the cancer before surgery as part of a plan intended to reduce the risk of it returning.

items.title: Why more than one phase?
items.text: Four 21-day cycles: paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15; carboplatin AUC 6 on Day 1. Four further cycles (cycles 5–8): doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 14 days. G-CSF support is required for every dose-dense AC cycle; the team prescribes its product and timing separately.

chapters.title: Tests and checks through treatment
chapters.intro: Ask who books each test, who reviews the result, and when you should hear the plan.

items.title: Blood tests
items.text: FBC, renal and liver tests weekly throughout chemotherapy, including review before each AC dose.

items.title: ECG and heart ultrasound
items.text: Baseline ECG under cardio-oncology guidance (not explicitly listed in NCCP 00348), and cardiac history/risk assessment. NCCP lists baseline echo/MUGA for age over 65 or when clinically indicated. Recheck the cardiac assessment before starting doxorubicin; echo/MUGA during treatment is driven by symptoms, risk or the agreed cardio-oncology plan. There is no automatic three-monthly echo schedule for every person on this pathway.

items.title: Thyroid and hormone checks
items.text: Thyroid and cortisol checks are not a routine immunotherapy schedule for this chemotherapy-only regimen. Investigate symptoms according to clinical need.

items.title: Scans and tumour markers
items.text: Record baseline breast/nodal findings and stage with imaging appropriate to the presentation. Assess clinical response during neoadjuvant treatment and use the appropriate breast imaging before surgery or sooner for concern. There is no universal three-monthly CT schedule for this early-breast pathway. After local treatment, arrange the agreed breast surveillance; routine CT/PET and tumour markers are not asymptomatic recurrence screening.

chapters.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and follow-up
chapters.intro: Other treatments depend on the complete diagnosis and pathology.

items.title: How the treatments fit
items.text: Chemotherapy comes before surgery. The surgeon discusses lumpectomy or mastectomy as alternatives according to your situation. Radiotherapy, if indicated, follows surgery and recovery; timing is agreed by both teams. It is not automatically given at the same time as these chemotherapy phases.

items.title: Hormone tablets and bone scans
items.text: This is a triple-negative pathway: endocrine therapy and endocrine-related DEXA are not automatically part of it. Bone-density testing may still be appropriate for other personal risk factors.

items.title: If symptoms or tests change
items.text: The team may pause, change or stop a medicine, reassess imaging or revise the surgical plan. Report concerns promptly.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, ECG and cardiac review, medicines review, fertility discussion where relevant and the consent conversation come first. The ECG recommendation is from ESC cardio-oncology guidance; NCCP 00348 explicitly lists risk-based echo/MUGA.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Trained staff check and access the line, give the prescribed premedicines and infusions, and monitor for reactions. Tell the nurse immediately about pain, burning, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: Visits include assessment, pharmacy preparation, premedicines, infusions and observation. The first visit and a change in phase can take longer. Ask about transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.
